title: How to Track Gravity Forms in GTM, Including Redirects and Enhanced Conversions
intro:
Gravity Forms is the form tool I run into most on client sites. Ten of the containers I checked this month run a Gravity Forms listener and nothing else, so when I test one, I want to be sure of what it's telling me.

So I submitted a clearly labelled test lead on a live site, with GTM Preview open. The form accepted it, sent me to a thank-you page, and the tracking caught it. gf_form_success fired and GA4 recorded it. That looks like a pass.

Then I opened the event. Name, email and phone were all gone. A leftover test setting in the container was removing them, and ec_phone was reading the email key anyway. Nothing in the setup looked broken, and I'd have missed it if I'd stopped when the event fired.

This walkthrough shows how to track Gravity Forms in GTM so you catch both problems: leads the usual recipe misses, and data that quietly goes missing.
tldr: Button clicks and thank-you pages can miscount your leads. This free script counts a Gravity Forms lead only when the form confirms it, even if the page reloads or redirects. Before going live, send one test lead and check that the email and phone are right.
sections: Why the usual Gravity Forms recipe misses leads

Search for this and you'll find the same listener in most guides: wait for gform_confirmation_loaded, then push an event. That event only fires when an AJAX form shows its confirmation on the same page. Gravity Forms can finish a submission three ways:

What the form doesgform_confirmation_loadedThis listener
AJAX confirmation on the pageFiresconfirmation_event or confirmation_class
Page reloads to a confirmationDoesn't fireDetects the confirmation with no form present
Redirects to a thank-you pageDoesn't firestored_recall, using data saved at submit

My test lead was the third kind. It redirected, so the usual recipe would have recorded nothing. Here's how the options I found compare:

OptionWhat it doesThe gap
Analytics Mania's guideThe clearest free guide: a listener for AJAX, a snippet for reloads, and a separate tutorial for redirectsReturns only the form ID, so no contact data
Optizent's guideA short tag on the same eventSends the form ID and doesn't cover redirects
Event Tracking for Gravity FormsFree WordPress plugin with GTM supportNo new features planned. Its page names the official Gravity Forms Google Analytics Add-on as the successor
ListenLayerHosted data layer platform with a Gravity Forms listenerYour tracking then depends on their platform

If you only need a count from AJAX forms, those guides are enough. I wanted all three outcomes, failed submissions and contact data from one GTM tag, without a WordPress plugin or editing each form's confirmation.
Before you start

Here's what you'll need:

  • GTM on the form pages and the thank-you page.
  • Publish access to the container.
  • Your GA4 Measurement ID, and your Google Ads conversion ID and label if you run ads.
  • A list of older Gravity Forms tags, thank-you triggers and any dataLayer.push snippets in form confirmations, because you'll remove them.

Does the site also use another form tool, or a landing page builder? Use the universal listener instead. Don't run both for Gravity Forms.
Step 1: Add the listener tag

1. Download the GTM tag, or get gravityforms-form-tracker.gtm.html from GitHub. It already has the <script> wrapper.
  2. In GTM, go to Tags > New > Custom HTML and paste it.
  3. Fire it on All Pages, including the thank-you page. That's where a redirected lead gets recorded.
[[img:gf-listener-tag|The listener on a live container, on All Pages.]]

To change the defaults, edit the config block at the top of the tag:

window.EC_FORM_CONFIG = {
  debug: false,             // true only while testing
  hashPii: false,           // true adds ec_email_sha256 and ec_phone_sha256
  rawFields: false,         // keeps ec_raw_fields out of the payload
  defaultCountryCode: '1',  // phone fallback
  countryCodeField: '',     // exact field name holding a country or dial code
  strictSuccess: false,     // true drops inferred successes
  extraThankYouPatterns: [] // add your thank-you URL if it isn't a common one
};
Check your thank-you URL. Redirects are recognised by common patterns such as thank-you, thanks and confirmation. If yours is something else, like /estimate-received, add it to extraThankYouPatterns or the lead won't be matched. If debug stays on, your console logs can show lead details, so turn it off before publishing.
Step 2: Create the trigger

The tag now pushes events, but nothing is listening yet. Go to Triggers > New > Custom Event and use the event name gf_form_success.

[[img:gf-trigger|One event, whichever way the form finished.]]

You can also add a trigger for gf_form_failed. It fires when Gravity Forms shows a validation message after someone has started the form, so an empty rage-click doesn't count. If a visitor fixes the error and resubmits, you'll see the failure and then the success.
Step 3: Send the lead to GA4

Create a Google Analytics: GA4 Event tag on that trigger, with form details as event parameters from Data Layer Variables: form_id, form_cta, form_position, form_platform and form_url.

[[img:uft-ga4-tag|Form details only. This one is from another account using the same pattern.]]
Keep contact details out of GA4. Never add ec_name, ec_email, ec_phone or ec_raw_fields here. GA4's terms prohibit personal data in event parameters. ec_raw_fields is off by default. If you turn it on, it holds every captured field.

Here's what the site from my test had in place:

[[img:gf-tag-list|The listener, a GA4 event on gf_form_success, and a separate generate_lead on the thank-you page. That last one can double count. Note the Consent Init tag at the top, which we'll come back to.]]

Pick one lead event for your GA4 reports. If you keep a thank-you page event as well, a refresh can count as a lead, which is what this listener is meant to avoid.

Register the parameters in GA4

GA4 collects these parameters, but you can't use them in reports until you register them. Go to Admin > Data display > Custom definitions > Create custom dimensions. Set the scope to Event, and enter each parameter exactly as the tag sends it:

Dimension nameEvent parameter
Form IDform_id
Form CTAform_cta
Form Positionform_position
Form Platformform_platform

Do this when you publish, because reports only fill in from events sent after the dimension exists. It can take 24 to 48 hours to show up, and you need Editor access on the property.

If you name your event form_submit, also turn off Form interactions in enhanced measurement. GA4 sends its own form_submit, so each lead could count twice.
Step 4: Add Google Ads and Enhanced Conversions

This is where the contact data matters. Create a Google Ads Conversion Tracking tag on the same trigger, and have a Conversion Linker on all pages. Then create these Data Layer Variables and a User-Provided Data variable set to Manual configuration:

Data Layer Variable nameUser-Provided Data field
ec_emailEmail
ec_phonePhone
[[img:uft-user-data|The variable with both fields mapped.]]
Open each variable and read its key. On the site I tested, the variable called Dlv - ec_phone had ec_email as its Data Layer Variable Name. The name looks right, so you won't see this in the variable list. Preview shows you the value, but only if there's a value to see.

The listener also pushes ec_first_name, ec_last_name and address keys when it can recognise the fields. Gravity Forms often names fields by number, like input_7.3, and on the form I tested the visitor's name landed in ec_name, with first and last empty. The ZIP was picked up as ec_postal_code. Check what your form gives you in Preview, and only map the keys that hold values.

For Meta, pass ec_event_id as the event ID so browser and server events are counted once.
Step 5: Check your consent settings

Now for the setting that caught my test lead. The listener auto-detects Google Consent Mode v2, OneTrust and Cookiebot. With analytics consent denied, nothing is stored, and events are held and replayed if consent is later granted. With personal data consent denied, events fire without contact data and carry ec_pii_redacted: true.

For testing or another consent tool, you can override that with a function:

window.EC_FORM_CONSENT_CHECK = function () {
  return { analytics: true, pii: false };
};
Remove this once you've finished testing. On the site I tested, this exact code was still in a Custom HTML tag called Consent Init, with a comment saying it was a test config, firing on every page. It overrides your real consent tool too. If you see a tag like that, open it and read what it returns.
Step 6: Test it, and open the event

Click Preview and connect to the site.

  1. Load a page with a form. Expect ec_tracker_initialized, with ec_forms_attached above 0.
  2. Run this in the console to see consent, attached forms and the last event:
    window._ecFormTrackers.gf.status()
  3. Submit with a required field empty. Expect gf_form_failed and no success.
  4. Fix it and submit a clearly labelled test lead. Expect one gf_form_success. If it redirects, look for it on the thank-you page.
  5. Click that event and read the Data Layer. ec_email and ec_phone should hold your test values, and ec_pii_redacted shouldn't be there.
  6. Refresh the thank-you page. Expect nothing new.
  7. If the page has two forms, submit each and check form_position.

Here's what a failed check looks like. This is my real test lead, and the event fired correctly:

[[img:gf-preview-redacted|The test lead on the live site: ec_pii_redacted is true, and Dlv - ec_email, ec_name and ec_phone are all undefined. Domain anonymised.]]

There's no error anywhere in that screen. The only signs are one extra line in the event and three undefined variables. Your test lead may also reach the client, so warn them first and use an obvious name and message.
Step 7: Publish, and clean up

Once the data is right, remove what the new tag replaces, then publish:

  • Older Gravity Forms tags and click or form-submit triggers.
  • Any dataLayer.push snippets in Gravity Forms confirmation text, which would fire a second event.
  • Thank-you page conversions for the same form, or each lead counts twice.

Then submit one more test lead with Preview closed, and check GA4 Realtime. If events appear in Preview but not live, check that a script optimiser like WP Rocket's delay JS or Cloudflare Rocket Loader isn't holding GTM back.

What you seeLikely causeFix

Phone holds an emailVariable reading the wrong keyStep 4
Nothing on a redirectThank-you URL not recognised, or on another domainextraThankYouPatterns. A different domain can't use stored data
Two success eventsAn old confirmation snippetStep 7
Two leads in GA4Thank-you event as well as gf_form_successStep 3
Works in Preview, not liveNot published, or GTM delayed by an optimiserStep 7
What I tested, and what to know

On a live site in November 2026, one labelled test lead on a form that redirects fired gf_form_success through stored_recall on v3.0.1, and showed the consent problem described here. I then loaded the current v3.3.0 on the same form with test values and my own consent setting, without sending a lead or reaching the site's tags. It returned the normalized email, phone and name. That's a test of the listener, and not proof that contact data reaches Google Ads. I've tested the listener with contact data on live forms too, and it works.

Limits to plan for:

  • A redirect to a different domain can't use the stored data.
  • Add-ons and themes can change Gravity Forms markup, so test on the live page.
  • Bot or spam submissions that pass Gravity Forms' validation still count.
  • Phone formatting is best effort. It assumes the default country code unless the number starts with +.
Frequently asked questions

Does this work with AJAX turned off?

Yes. Reloads and redirects are both covered, which is the main reason to use it over a gform_confirmation_loaded listener.

Why not GTM's built-in Form Submission trigger?

Analytics Mania's guide says it rarely works with Gravity Forms, and it can't tell whether Gravity Forms accepted the lead.

Do I need to edit my forms?

No. Everything runs from GTM, and you can remove old confirmation snippets.

Should I turn on hashPii?

Only if something needs SHA-256 values in the dataLayer. Google tags can hash plain values themselves.

Is it free?

Yes, MIT licensed and on GitHub.
closing: If you'd rather have this installed and checked for you, or your lead numbers still don't add up after following this guide, I can help.
